title: Gall's Law: Why Over-Engineered Productivity Systems Always Fail
alt_title_1: Stop Building 20-Tab Notion Dashboards on Day One
alt_title_2: The 1975 Systems Law Every Solo Builder Needs
description_hook: In 1975, systems theorist John Gall explained why complex systems designed from scratch always collapse - and why starting with a stupidly simple Version 1.0 is the only path to durable daily output.

scenes.headline: Why 20-Tab Dashboards Die by Thursday
bullets: Color-coding templates feels like productive progress
Complex friction kills execution the first busy week
scenes.narration: If you spent all weekend building a twenty-tab productivity dashboard and stopped using it by Thursday, a nineteen seventy-five engineering rule explains why.

scenes.headline: John Gall's 1975 Law of Working Systems
bullets: Every working complex system grew out of a simple one
Systems designed complicated on Day 1 never survive
scenes.narration: Systems theorist John Gall put it in his 1975 book Systemantics: a complex system that works has always evolved from a simple system that worked. A complex system designed from scratch never works.

scenes.headline: Designing From Scratch vs Evolving Through Reps
scenes.right_body: 1 index card + 1 daily block -> evolved over 90 days
scenes.narration: Beginners break this rule constantly. They design twelve-step morning routines and complicated automation pipelines before they have even shipped a single piece of finished work.

scenes.headline: Build for Your Most Exhausted Tuesday
scenes.stat_subtext: 1 checklist • 1 focus block • Upgrade only real bottlenecks
scenes.narration: Flip the sequence: start with one plain checklist, one daily focus block, and one repeatable workflow you can execute even on your most exhausting Tuesday.

scenes.headline: Earn Complexity After 30 Days of Consistency
bullets: Consistency beats clever architecture every week
Add automation only when manual reps work smoothly
scenes.narration: Earn the right to add complexity only after thirty days of simple wins - otherwise, do not be surprised...
scenes.source: Mind & Margin rule of thumb (advice, not a study)
